incidents.title: Hungary: a ruling-party mayor forcibly removes Telex reporters from a campaign event
incidents.summary: A mayor from Hungary's ruling Fidesz party physically removed two Telex journalists from a campaign forum in a community center, covering their camera lens and pushing them out after they declined to leave what he called a closed event.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Telex, an independent Hungarian outlet, was covering a campaign forum ahead of Hungary's April 2026 parliamentary election when the mayor hosting the event moved to stop the reporting.
incidents.what_happened: On March 10, 2026, Telex correspondent Judit Presinszky and camera operator Nora Siteri went to a campaign forum for the ruling Fidesz party in a community center in Csakbereny, central Hungary. Mayor Laszlo Vecsei, who was hosting the event, grabbed Siteri's camera to cover the lens and then pushed the journalists, grabbing one of them by the arm, before they were removed from the building. A member of a local civilian patrol group then prevented the pair from re-entering. Vecsei said he acted after the journalists refused to leave what he described as a closed, non-public campaign event, though Telex said it was covering a public function open to constituents. Telex said it had filed a criminal complaint over the removal. The Committee to Protect Journalists said the episode marked a new low for a Hungarian press corps that already faces years of exclusion from government events under Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
incidents.stated_justification: Mayor Vecsei said he removed the journalists "after they refused to leave what he described as a closed, non-public campaign event."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Telex's reporters were prevented from covering the campaign forum in person and were physically blocked from returning to the building, and the outlet turned to a criminal complaint rather than continued on-site reporting.
incidents.status: Telex has filed a criminal complaint over the removal; no outcome of that complaint has been reported.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: It is not established in the sources reviewed whether the criminal complaint led to any charge against Mayor Vecsei.
incidents.outcome_note: Telex filed a criminal complaint the same period as the removal; the Committee to Protect Journalists reports no resolution of that complaint.
incidents.ladder_note: A government official used physical force to remove and bar named reporters from an event, rather than only denying a credential or building pass.

incidents.title: Russia: entry bans, visa restrictions and bureau closures for foreign correspondents
incidents.summary: Over several months in 2022, Russian authorities closed a Canadian broadcaster's Moscow bureau, barred dozens of named British and Australian journalists from entering the country, and suspended simplified visa rules for European journalists.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Russia's actions followed Western governments' sanctions on Russian state broadcasters and officials after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
incidents.what_happened: Across the spring of 2022, Russian authorities took a series of steps to keep foreign journalists out of the country. On May 18, Russian authorities moved to close CBC/Radio-Canada's Moscow bureau and cancel the visa and accreditation of its journalists, matching Canada's decision to bar Russian state television. On June 14, Russia barred 49 British citizens, including 29 named journalists, from entering the country. Two days later, it barred 121 Australians, including journalists from ABC News, the Sydney Morning Herald, Nine News and Sky News. Separately, President Vladimir Putin signed a law suspending simplified visa procedures for several categories of visitors, including journalists, coming from most European countries. Russian officials framed each step as a response matching measures taken by the country concerned against Russian state media or officials, rather than as a general press policy.
incidents.stated_justification: Russian officials presented the entry bans on British and Australian journalists as a response matching measures the United Kingdom and Australia had taken against Russian journalists and officials; a specific legal justification beyond that framing was not detailed in the source reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Named journalists from CBC, the BBC, the Sydney Morning Herald and other outlets lost the ability to report from inside Russia in person, and foreign outlets lost simplified visa access for future correspondents.
incidents.status: The entry bans and visa restrictions remained in force through 2022 with no indication of reversal in the source reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not give a complete published list of the 29 British or the Australian journalists named, or confirm whether any individual ban was later lifted.
incidents.outcome_note: The bans on named British and Australian journalists and the suspension of simplified visas for European journalists remained in effect through 2022 according to the source reviewed.
incidents.ladder_note: Dozens of named foreign correspondents were barred from entering the country by law and by sanction, not merely excluded from one building or briefing.

incidents.title: China: three Wall Street Journal correspondents expelled over an opinion headline
incidents.summary: China's foreign ministry expelled three Wall Street Journal correspondents and revoked their press credentials after an opinion column, unrelated to their own reporting, used a headline the ministry called offensive.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Wall Street Journal had published an opinion column on February 3, 2020, by an outside scholar, headlined "China Is the Real Sick Man of Asia," about the economic effects of the coronavirus outbreak.
incidents.what_happened: On February 19, 2020, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs ordered three Wall Street Journal correspondents in Beijing, deputy bureau chief Josh Chin and reporters Chao Deng and Philip Wen, to leave the country within five days and revoked their press credentials. The order came more than two weeks after the newspaper ran an opinion column by an outside academic, Hudson Institute scholar Walter Russell Mead, under the headline "China Is the Real Sick Man of Asia," discussing the coronavirus outbreak's economic effects. None of the three expelled journalists had written or edited the column. Foreign ministry spokesperson Geng Shuang called the headline "racist" and cited it as the basis for the expulsions. The Wall Street Journal's own reporters had separately criticized the headline as a poor editorial choice, but the paper declined to apologize on the newsroom's behalf for a piece written by an unrelated outside contributor.
incidents.stated_justification: Foreign ministry spokesperson Geng Shuang characterized the opinion headline as "racist" and cited it as the basis for revoking the journalists' press credentials.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Three working Wall Street Journal correspondents lost their accreditation and were made to leave China within five days over content that none of them had written, reducing the paper's Beijing reporting capacity during the early coronavirus outbreak.
incidents.status: The expulsions were carried out as ordered; the source reviewed does not report any reversal.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: It is not stated in the source reviewed whether any of the three journalists were later permitted to return to China on assignment.
incidents.outcome_note: The three journalists' press credentials were revoked and the expulsion carried out; no reversal is reported in the source reviewed.
incidents.ladder_note: Working correspondents were expelled from the country over content written by someone outside their newsroom, not barred from one building or event.

incidents.title: Belarus: accreditation withdrawn from 17 journalists working for foreign outlets
incidents.summary: Belarus's government revoked the accreditation of at least 17 journalists working for foreign outlets, including the BBC, Reuters, the Associated Press, Radio Liberty, AFP and Deutsche Welle, as they covered protests after a disputed presidential election.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The journalists had been covering protests that followed Belarus's August 9, 2020, presidential election, which the opposition and Western governments said was falsified in favor of Alexander Lukashenko.
incidents.what_happened: On August 29, 2020, Belarusian authorities revoked the accreditation of at least 17 journalists who had been covering the post-election protests for foreign media outlets, among them the BBC, Reuters, the Associated Press, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Agence France-Presse and Deutsche Welle. Government spokesman Anatoly Glaz said the accreditation withdrawals followed a recommendation from Belarus's counter-terrorism unit. Some of the affected foreign journalists were deported to Russia the same day. The move came three weeks after Belarus's disputed presidential election, which had drawn large street protests and a heavy police response, and left foreign wire services and broadcasters largely unable to report from inside the country on the unrest as it continued into the autumn.
incidents.stated_justification: Government spokesman Anatoly Glaz said "the decision to revoke the media accreditations was made after a recommendation by Belarus's counter-terrorism unit."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: At least 17 journalists working for major international wire services and broadcasters lost their ability to report from inside Belarus, and some were deported the same day.
incidents.status: The accreditation withdrawals took effect immediately and some journalists were deported; the source reviewed does not report a reversal.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not name all 17 affected journalists or state whether any of them later regained accreditation.
incidents.outcome_note: The accreditation of at least 17 journalists was withdrawn and some were deported the same day, with no reversal reported in the source reviewed.
incidents.ladder_note: At least 17 journalists working for named international outlets lost accreditation nationwide and some were deported, not confined to one building or pool.

incidents.title: Philippines: a Rappler reporter is barred from the presidential palace
incidents.summary: President Rodrigo Duterte ordered Rappler reporter Pia Ranada and the outlet's CEO barred from Malacanang Palace, the seat of the Philippine presidency, after the government revoked Rappler's operating license.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The ban followed the Philippine Securities and Exchange Commission's January 2018 revocation of Rappler's operating license over a foreign-ownership finding, a decision Rappler said was really aimed at its critical coverage of Duterte.
incidents.what_happened: On February 21, 2018, Jhopee Avancena, head of Malacanang Palace's internal house affairs office, told Rappler reporter Pia Ranada by text message that she and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa had been banned from the palace grounds on President Duterte's orders. Ranada was initially denied access by guards at the gate but was eventually allowed to join a televised news briefing that day. Presidential spokesperson Harry Roque said the government acted because Duterte had lost trust in Rappler over what he called "fake news" reporting, and said Rappler's reporters would have to cover the president's speeches and activities by television rather than in person from the palace. The ban followed weeks of government pressure on Rappler, including the Securities and Exchange Commission's revocation of its operating license the previous month, a decision widely read as retribution for the outlet's coverage of Duterte's campaign and his anti-drug enforcement policy.
incidents.stated_justification: Presidential spokesperson Harry Roque said the government banned Rappler's reporters because President Duterte had "lost trust" in the outlet's "fake news" reporting.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Rappler's palace correspondent could no longer cover the president's activities in person and the outlet was told to rely on television broadcasts instead of first-hand access.
incidents.status: The ban remained in force for the remainder of Duterte's term; no reversal is reported in the source reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not state whether the ban was lifted after Duterte left office in mid-2022.
incidents.outcome_note: The source reviewed reports only the ban taking effect and does not state whether or when it ended.
incidents.ladder_note: The head of government personally ordered a named outlet's reporters excluded from the seat of government after revoking the outlet's corporate license.

incidents.title: Turkiye: the presidency's press card system is found restrictive by the country's top administrative court
incidents.summary: Turkiye's Council of State suspended 2018 rules under which the presidency's Communications Directorate could deny or cancel the yellow and turquoise press cards that let reporters work and enter official buildings, after finding the grounds for denial too broad.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The 2018 rules had let the presidency cancel press cards for vaguely worded reasons, including "diminishing the dignity of the media profession," and had been used against journalists dismissed or reassigned after the 2016 coup attempt.
incidents.what_happened: Since 2018, Turkiye's presidency, through its Communications Directorate, has controlled the issuance and cancellation of the country's yellow and turquoise press cards, which let journalists enter official buildings and access official information. The rules allowed cancellation for broadly worded reasons, including "diminishing the dignity of the media profession" or acting against national security. On April 1, 2021, Turkiye's Council of State, the country's highest administrative court, suspended the 2018 regulation, finding its grounds for denial and cancellation too broad. By the time of the ruling, staff at the newspaper Evrensel had waited more than two years for replacement cards, journalist Canan Coskun had lost eligibility after moving from print to a digital outlet, and no staff member at Mezopotamya News Agency held a card at all. A journalists' union chair said about 300 journalists were awaiting a decision on reapplications. The presidency said it would keep provisions aimed at journalists it accused of "making propaganda" for "terrorism."
incidents.stated_justification: The presidency said of the underlying 2018 rules that "the clauses that prevent those who make propaganda for terrorism and violence from hiding behind the press card were strengthened."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists at outlets including Evrensel and Mezopotamya News Agency were left without valid press cards for years, restricting their access to official buildings and information even after the court's ruling.
incidents.status: The Council of State suspended the 2018 regulation in April 2021, but hundreds of journalists' reapplications remained pending.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not report how many of the roughly 300 pending reapplications were ultimately approved.
incidents.outcome_note: Turkiye's Council of State suspended the challenged 2018 press card regulation, though the source reviewed reports hundreds of journalists still waiting for cards afterward.
incidents.ladder_note: A national regulator controlled the credential every journalist needs to work and enter official buildings, denying or delaying cards for hundreds of reporters for years.

incidents.title: Zimbabwe: the High Court refuses to accredit Daily News journalists under the media registration law
incidents.summary: Zimbabwe's High Court ruled that Daily News journalists could not be accredited to work as reporters until their newspaper's publisher had itself been registered with the government's Media and Information Commission.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Daily News, Zimbabwe's largest independent newspaper, had been closed since September 2003 after the Supreme Court found it unregistered under the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA), a 2002 law requiring every media outlet and journalist to register with the government.
incidents.what_happened: On May 12, 2005, a judge on Zimbabwe's High Court ruled that journalists at the Daily News could not receive individual accreditation to practice as reporters until the newspaper's publisher, Associated Newspapers of Zimbabwe (ANZ), had first been granted registration by the government's Media and Information Commission (MIC), the body created under AIPPA to register media outlets and license journalists. The ruling came during ANZ's long-running effort to reopen the paper, which police had shut in September 2003. At a hearing five days earlier, the MIC had requested additional documents from ANZ, and the company's lawyer said the commission had demanded information beyond what the law required. The Committee to Protect Journalists' executive director at the time, Ann Cooper, said the accreditation process amounted to a means of providing cover for a government campaign against the independent press, rather than a genuine licensing procedure.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed; the Media and Information Commission did not issue a public statement explaining the additional documents it requested from the newspaper's publisher.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Daily News journalists remained unable to work as accredited reporters because the newspaper's publisher itself could not obtain registration, keeping Zimbabwe's largest independent paper off the newsstands.
incidents.status: The accreditation refusal stood as of the ruling; the Daily News did not reopen for several more years.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not explain what additional documents the Media and Information Commission required or why the registration was withheld.
incidents.outcome_note: The High Court upheld the requirement that the publisher be registered before its journalists could be accredited; the paper was not relicensed until 2010.
incidents.ladder_note: Journalists at a named newspaper were denied the individual credential needed to work at all, conditioned on a separate corporate registration the government withheld for years.

incidents.title: Kazakhstan: new accreditation rules let officials withdraw a journalist's pass for off-topic questions
incidents.summary: Kazakhstan's government adopted rules allowing journalists' accreditation to be withdrawn for six months over conduct at a news event, including asking off-topic questions, while proposing separate rules letting the foreign ministry deny foreign media accreditation over any violation of Kazakh law.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The rules followed a period of monthslong accreditation denials against journalists with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Kazakh service, Radio Azattyq, and escalating administrative charges against them for allegedly spreading false information.
incidents.what_happened: New domestic media rules took effect in Kazakhstan on August 20, 2024, allowing a journalist's accreditation to be withdrawn for six months if they twice failed to comply with rules at news events, a category that could include asking questions considered off-topic. A day earlier, the foreign ministry had posted proposed rules that would let it deny or revoke accreditation for foreign correspondents over any violation of Kazakh law, including minor administrative offenses. The rules followed a period in which domestic journalists and correspondents for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Kazakh service, Radio Azattyq, faced monthslong denials of accreditation alongside a rising number of administrative charges accusing them of spreading false information. The Committee to Protect Journalists said it emailed Kazakhstan's Ministry of Culture and Information and Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment but received no reply from either.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed; Kazakhstan's Ministry of Culture and Information and Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to requests for comment on the new rules.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists with Radio Azattyq and other domestic reporters faced accreditation denials lasting months even before the new rules, restricting their access to official events and information.
incidents.status: The domestic rules took effect August 20, 2024, and the foreign media rules remained proposed as of the source's publication.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not report how many journalists lost accreditation for six months under the new domestic rule once it took effect.
incidents.outcome_note: The domestic accreditation rule had taken effect and the foreign media rule remained proposed, with officials not responding to requests for comment.
incidents.ladder_note: A government rule lets officials withdraw a journalist's accreditation for the content of the questions asked, not only for building or event access.

incidents.title: China: press credentials and visas withheld from correspondents at three American newspapers
incidents.summary: A survey by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of China found the government refused new press credentials to journalists tied to American outlets and cancelled or refused visas for correspondents at the New York Times, Wall Street Journal and Washington Post through 2020.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The findings covered a year in which China expelled dozens of foreign journalists amid tit-for-tat measures with the United States and additional restrictions tied to the coronavirus outbreak.
incidents.what_happened: In a report issued in March 2021 covering the preceding year, the Foreign Correspondents' Club of China (FCCC), a professional association of foreign reporters based in the country, surveyed 150 of its members from 30 countries and regions and found that media freedom for foreign correspondents had deteriorated significantly in 2020. Among the specific findings, the report said Chinese authorities had refused to issue press credentials to journalists accredited with United States news outlets, had cancelled and refused to issue new visas for correspondents at the New York Times, Wall Street Journal and Washington Post, and had expelled at least 18 foreign journalists in the first half of the year alone. The credential and visa restrictions extended the effect of earlier expulsion orders, since a journalist without a valid press card or visa cannot legally remain in the country to report, regardless of whether they were personally named in an expulsion order.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed; no Chinese government justification for the specific credential and visa denials is quoted in the source.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Correspondents at three major American newspapers lost the credentials and visas needed to report from China even where they had not been individually ordered to leave, compounding earlier expulsions.
incidents.status: The restrictions were in force through the period covered by the March 2021 report; the source reviewed does not report a reversal.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not say how many correspondents at the three newspapers were affected by name or whether any later regained credentials.
incidents.outcome_note: The credential and visa denials were in force for the year covered by the survey, with no reversal reported in the source reviewed.
incidents.ladder_note: Credentials and visas needed to work at all were denied to correspondents at three named outlets on a national scale, on top of earlier individual expulsion orders.

incidents.title: Russia: a Moscow court suspends Novaya Gazeta's print license
incidents.summary: A Moscow court suspended the print license of Novaya Gazeta, whose editor Dmitry Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize, after the media regulator Roskomnadzor said the paper had not provided documents about a 2006 change of ownership.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The suspension came about six months into Russia's invasion of Ukraine, during which several independent Russian outlets closed or moved abroad rather than operate under new wartime speech laws.
incidents.what_happened: On September 5, 2022, Moscow's Basmanny District Court suspended the print license of Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia's last major independent newspapers, at the request of Roskomnadzor, the state media regulator. Roskomnadzor alleged the paper had failed to provide documents relating to a change of ownership that had taken place in 2006, sixteen years earlier. Novaya Gazeta's editor, Dmitry Muratov, who had shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize for his work at the paper, called the suspension "a political hit job, without the slightest legal basis." The newspaper itself said on social media that the authorities had effectively ended the publication and taken thirty years of its staff's work. The suspension followed Novaya Gazeta's earlier decision, days after Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, to pause its print and online publishing rather than operate under new laws criminalizing what the government called false information about the military.
incidents.stated_justification: Roskomnadzor alleged the newspaper "failed to provide documents relating to a change of ownership in 2006."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: One of Russia's last major independent newspapers lost its print license entirely, ending decades of publication under a legal pretext its editor said had no basis.
incidents.status: The print license remained suspended as of the ruling; the source reviewed does not report a reversal.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not explain why a 2006 ownership matter was raised only in 2022 or what documents Roskomnadzor said were missing.
incidents.outcome_note: The Basmanny District Court's suspension of the print license stood as of the ruling, with no reversal reported in the source reviewed.
incidents.ladder_note: A national court ended a Nobel-recognized newspaper's print license outright over a sixteen-year-old paperwork dispute, not a temporary suspension or fine.

incidents.title: China (Hong Kong): Apple Daily closes after its assets are frozen under the national security law
incidents.summary: Apple Daily, Hong Kong's largest pro-democracy newspaper, printed its final edition after the government froze its parent company's assets and arrested its editors under the national security law imposed on the territory in 2020.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The closure followed Hong Kong's 2019 to 2020 pro-democracy protests and Beijing's imposition of a national security law on the territory in June 2020, which criminalized broadly defined acts of subversion and collusion with foreign forces.
incidents.what_happened: Apple Daily, a Hong Kong newspaper founded by media owner Jimmy Lai and known for its pro-democracy coverage, printed its final edition in June 2021 after Hong Kong police froze the assets of its parent company, Next Digital, under the national security law and arrested several of its senior editors. Lai himself had already been detained and was, as of a December 2021 report, serving a separate 20-month prison term related to a conviction for his part in unauthorized demonstrations, while also awaiting trial on national security and fraud charges. On December 28, 2021, Hong Kong's Department of Justice filed further conspiracy charges accusing Lai and six former Apple Daily executives, including former chief executive Cheung Kim Hung and former editor-in-chief Ryan Law Wai-kwong, of printing seditious publications, a charge that could bring up to three years in prison on top of any national security sentence, which could reach life imprisonment.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated directly in the source reviewed; Hong Kong's security bureau, in a related statement about the sedition case, described Apple Daily's sister outlet Stand News as pursuing an editorial line it called intended to "smear and vilify" the authorities, a characterization the government applied to the wider media prosecutions of this period.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Hong Kong's largest pro-democracy newspaper stopped publishing entirely after twenty-six years, and several of its most senior editors faced prosecution that could carry sentences up to life imprisonment.
incidents.status: Apple Daily remained closed and its former executives faced additional charges as of the report reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not give the exact date of Next Digital's asset freeze or state the final outcome of the national security charges against Lai and the other executives.
incidents.outcome_note: Apple Daily did not resume publication and its former executives faced additional charges as of the December 2021 report reviewed.
incidents.ladder_note: A newspaper's assets were frozen and its senior editors charged with offenses carrying up to life imprisonment, ending publication entirely rather than a licensing dispute or fine.

incidents.title: Venezuela: the government declines to renew RCTV's broadcast concession
incidents.summary: Venezuela's government let Radio Caracas Television's twenty-year broadcast concession expire rather than renew it, replacing the country's most-watched channel with a new state broadcaster; a regional human rights court later found the decision violated free expression.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: President Hugo Chavez's government accused RCTV of supporting the failed April 2002 coup attempt against him, an accusation the government cited alongside the concession's scheduled expiration.
incidents.what_happened: Radio Caracas Television's twenty-year broadcast concession was due to expire at midnight on May 27, 2007, and Venezuela's government, led by President Hugo Chavez, chose not to renew it. A new state broadcaster, the Venezuelan Social Television Station, took over RCTV's former frequency. Government officials accused RCTV's employees of having supported the failed 2002 coup against Chavez, and separately accused the channel of violating Venezuelan law and broadcasting indecent content; the administration described the non-renewal as the natural result of the concession's expiration rather than a deliberate act against the channel. In September 2015, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled that the non-renewal had in fact violated freedom of expression, finding it was "a restriction on the exercise of freedom of expression designed to impede the communication and circulation of ideas and opinions" and that the government's real purpose was to stop RCTV's critical coverage of Chavez's administration. The court said the decision had also harmed the public's right to access RCTV's editorial line.
incidents.stated_justification: The government described the non-renewal as "natural and inexorable," the automatic result of the concession's expiration, while separately accusing RCTV's staff of having backed the 2002 coup.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Venezuela's most-watched television channel went off the open airwaves entirely, replaced by a state broadcaster, ending its national terrestrial reach.
incidents.status: RCTV did not return to open-signal broadcasting; it continued only through cable and international channels.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not state whether Venezuela complied with the 2015 Inter-American Court ruling by taking any specific remedial action.
incidents.outcome_note: A regional human rights court found in 2015 that the 2007 non-renewal violated free expression, but the source reviewed does not report RCTV's return to open-signal broadcasting.
incidents.ladder_note: The country's most-watched television channel lost its national broadcast concession entirely, later found by an international court to have been aimed at ending its critical coverage.

incidents.title: Zimbabwe: police close the Daily News under the media registration law
incidents.summary: Zimbabwe's Supreme Court ruled the Daily News, the country's largest independent newspaper, was operating unregistered under a 2002 media law, and police shut its offices the next day; the paper stayed closed for nearly seven years.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The closure came amid a wider campaign by President Robert Mugabe's government against independent media following the contested 2002 presidential election.
incidents.what_happened: On September 11, 2003, Zimbabwe's Supreme Court declared that the Daily News was violating the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA), a 2002 law requiring every media company to register with the government's Media and Information Commission (MIC). Because the paper's publisher had not registered, the court said it was operating outside the law and would consider constitutional arguments only after registration took place. The next day, police raided the newspaper's offices and ordered all journalists to leave the building, citing the Supreme Court's declaration. Administrative courts twice later ordered the Media and Information Commission to register the Daily News, but police closed the offices again each time journalists tried to resume work. Government officials said they were not interfering in the judicial process, while describing the independent press as serving foreign interests. The paper did not print again until the Media Commission granted it a new license in May 2010, nearly seven years later.
incidents.stated_justification: Government officials said the courts, not the government, were responsible for the closure, while describing the independent press as serving outside interests; the source reviewed does not quote a specific legal justification beyond the registration requirement.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Zimbabwe's largest independent newspaper was unable to publish for nearly seven years, and journalists were physically removed from its offices each time they attempted to resume work.
incidents.status: The paper was closed from September 2003 until it received a new license in May 2010.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not explain why the Media and Information Commission twice failed to comply with administrative court orders to register the paper.
incidents.outcome_note: Zimbabwe's Media Commission granted the Daily News a new publishing license on May 27, 2010, nearly seven years after the closure.
incidents.ladder_note: The country's largest independent newspaper was shut by police and kept off newsstands for nearly seven years, not a temporary suspension or fine.

incidents.title: Hungary: Klubradio loses its terrestrial broadcast license over its tender application
incidents.summary: Hungary's Media Council ended Klubradio's decades-old terrestrial broadcast license, citing errors in its renewal application, after the station had built a following as one of the country's few remaining independent voices.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The decision affected one of the last Hungarian broadcasters to carry news and talk programming independent of the government of Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
incidents.what_happened: Hungary's Media Council, the country's broadcast regulator known as the NMHH, denied Klubradio's license renewal in September 2020, and the station's terrestrial broadcasting ceased in February 2021 once its old license expired. The council said Klubradio's tender application contained incorrect, incomplete and contradictory submissions, pointing to specific issues such as an incompletely filled-out form and a program length recorded as 45 minutes rather than 50. The council also questioned the sustainability of a business model relying on listener donations. Klubradio's owner, Andras Arato, acknowledged one of the errors, saying the station had failed to complete a form correctly, but argued the underlying decision was aimed at the station's independent voice. Hungary's highest court, the Curia, upheld the Media Council's decision in September 2021. Klubradio has continued broadcasting online since losing its terrestrial signal.
incidents.stated_justification: The Media Council said Klubradio's tender submission was "incorrect, incomplete and contradictory," and that it was Klubradio's own application, not the council, that ended the station's terrestrial service.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: One of Hungary's few remaining independent broadcasters lost its terrestrial frequency, keeping its programming from radio listeners who did not seek it out online.
incidents.status: Hungary's Curia upheld the license denial in September 2021, and Klubradio has broadcast online only since losing its terrestrial signal.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not report whether other broadcasters' tender applications with similar errors received the same treatment.
incidents.outcome_note: Hungary's Curia upheld the Media Council's denial of Klubradio's license renewal in September 2021.
incidents.ladder_note: A national broadcast regulator ended one of the country's last independent stations' terrestrial license over its paperwork, and the country's top court upheld the decision.

incidents.title: Cambodia: Prime Minister Hun Sen orders Voice of Democracy's license revoked over one article
incidents.summary: Prime Minister Hun Sen personally ordered the license of independent outlet Voice of Democracy revoked over an article about an earthquake-aid agreement signed by his son, rejecting the outlet's published apology.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The article, published February 8, 2023, reported that Hun Sen's son and eventual successor, Hun Manet, had overstepped his authority by signing a $100,000 earthquake aid agreement for Turkiye.
incidents.what_happened: On February 12, 2023, Prime Minister Hun Sen said Voice of Democracy had defamed him and his son Hun Manet in a February 8 article alleging Hun Manet exceeded his authority by signing a $100,000 earthquake aid agreement with Turkiye. Hun Sen initially demanded the outlet verify its facts and apologize within 72 hours. When Voice of Democracy published a further apology on the morning of February 13, Hun Sen said on social media that he was standing by his order to revoke its license, and the Ministry of Information revoked it that day. Voice of Democracy's associate editor, Ananth Baliga, said the closure of independent media would leave corruption unchecked and let those in power act without restraint. The outlet had operated for more than a decade as one of Cambodia's few independent Khmer- and English-language news sources.
incidents.stated_justification: Hun Sen said Voice of Democracy "intentionally slandered him and his son Hun Manet" in the February 8 article about the earthquake aid agreement.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: One of Cambodia's few remaining independent news outlets lost its operating license entirely over a single article, ending more than a decade of publication.
incidents.status: The license revocation took effect February 13, 2023; the source reviewed does not report a reversal.

incidents.title: Israel: a court bars any mention of the 'Prisoner X' case
incidents.summary: An Israeli judge ordered Israeli media barred from any mention of a prisoner held under a false identity, or of the order itself, applying a system under which security-related stories must be reviewed and cleared by the military before publication.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The order concerned the custody of a man later identified as Ben Zygier, an Australian-Israeli detained on suspicion of harming state security, whose case Israeli outlets could not report on for years under the order.
incidents.what_happened: In June 2010, Israeli district court judge Hila Gerstl issued a court order banning any mention of a prisoner who came to be known publicly only as "Prisoner X," or of the circumstances of his custody, and separately prohibited any mention that the order itself existed. The order operated alongside Israel's long-standing military review system, under which all news publications dealing with security issues must be approved in advance by a military reviewing authority before publication, a standard Israel's High Court has said requires proof that publication would cause imminent, certain and actual harm to state security. Israeli authorities separately maintained an informal Editors' Committee, through which the prime minister's office asked media heads not to publish information described as very embarrassing to a government agency in exchange for advance notice of such information; Haaretz editor-in-chief Aluf Benn declined to take part, saying the arrangement would turn editors into intelligence assets rather than independent journalists.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed as a specific published order; Israel's general standard for pre-publication military review, as set by the High Court, requires proof that publication would cause "imminent, certain, and actual harm to state security."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Israeli media were barred from reporting on the prisoner's case at all for years, and could not even acknowledge that a court order existed, while Israel's wider military review system required advance approval for any security-related story.
incidents.status: The order remained in force inside Israel for years; the case became publicly known only through international reporting.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not state when or how the domestic order was eventually narrowed or lifted.
incidents.outcome_note: The source reviewed, a 2013 annual survey, documents the order's existence and Israel's wider military review system without stating when the domestic order was resolved.
incidents.ladder_note: A court order barred any domestic mention of a named prisoner's case or of the order itself, backed by a standing system requiring advance approval of security reporting.

incidents.title: Turkiye: the broadcast regulator fines and suspends channels for earthquake coverage
incidents.summary: Turkiye's broadcast regulator, RTUK, fined three television channels and suspended the next five episodes of two of their programs after they aired criticism of the government's response to the February 2023 earthquakes.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Earthquakes in southern Turkiye in early February 2023 killed more than 50,000 people and drew widespread criticism of the government's building codes and disaster response.
incidents.what_happened: On February 22, 2023, Turkiye's Radio and Television Supreme Council (RTUK), the state broadcast regulator, fined three television channels, Halk TV and TELE1 at five percent of their January revenue each and FOX TV Turkiye at three percent, over broadcasts criticizing the government's response to earthquakes that had struck the country weeks earlier and killed tens of thousands of people. RTUK also suspended the next five episodes of the specific Halk TV and TELE1 programs that had aired the criticism, barring those programs from airing at all for that period regardless of content. The Committee to Protect Journalists said it emailed RTUK for comment but received no response, and called for the fines and suspensions to be revoked, saying critical journalism during a period of mourning could be harsh but could also help bring about accountability.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed; RTUK did not respond to a request for comment on its reasoning for the fines and suspensions.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Three broadcasters were fined over their earthquake coverage and two had specific programs barred from airing for five future episodes regardless of content, a forward-looking restriction on what they could broadcast next.
incidents.status: The fines and program suspensions were imposed and, as of the source reviewed, had not been revoked.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not report whether the fines were paid or challenged in court.
incidents.outcome_note: CPJ called for the penalties to be revoked; the source reviewed does not report that RTUK did so.
incidents.ladder_note: A national regulator barred two programs from airing at all for five future episodes over their earthquake coverage, a forward restriction rather than a single broadcast ban.

incidents.title: Egypt: a license requirement leaves an independent news site unable to operate legally for years
incidents.summary: Egypt's Supreme Council for Media Regulation required news websites to obtain a government license to operate, and independent outlet Al-Manassa's application, filed in 2018, went unanswered for more than two years.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The licensing requirement operated alongside a 2018 cybercrime law that made it a crime to use certain software tools without the council's permission, according to Al-Manassa's editor.
incidents.what_happened: Egypt's Supreme Council for Media Regulation (SCMR), founded in 2018 to oversee print, broadcast and online media, required news websites operating in the country to obtain a license from it before they could publish legally. Al-Manassa, an independent Egyptian news site founded in 2016, submitted its license application in October 2018 when the council called for websites to register, but had received no response as of an October 2020 interview with its editor, Nora Younis, meaning the outlet had operated for two years under an unresolved licensing requirement with no legal certainty about its status. Younis also said Egypt's cybercrime law separately made it a criminal offense to use certain open-source software tools without the council's permission if doing so could be characterized as committing a crime, a provision she said gave authorities broad discretion over online publishers' technical operations as well as their editorial content.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed; the Supreme Council for Media Regulation did not respond to Al-Manassa's 2018 license application or explain the delay.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: An independent news site operated for more than two years without a resolved license, unable to obtain the legal certainty the licensing system was meant to provide, under a regulator that could also treat unlicensed software use as a crime.
incidents.status: As of the October 2020 interview, Al-Manassa's 2018 application remained unanswered.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not state whether the Supreme Council for Media Regulation ever responded to Al-Manassa's application.
incidents.outcome_note: Al-Manassa's editor said the outlet's 2018 license application had received no response as of the October 2020 interview.
incidents.ladder_note: A national council required a license before a news site could operate at all and left the application unanswered for years rather than approving, denying or fining it.

incidents.title: Russia: journalist Ivan Safronov is sentenced to 22 years for treason
incidents.summary: A Russian court sentenced military correspondent Ivan Safronov to 22 years in prison for treason, accusing him of spying for a foreign state, in a case his supporters linked to his 2019 reporting on Russian arms sales to Egypt.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Safronov had reported for the newspapers Kommersant and Vedomosti on Russian military affairs, including 2019 coverage of a planned sale of fighter jets to Egypt, before taking a communications role at Russia's space agency.
incidents.what_happened: On September 5, 2022, a Moscow court sentenced Ivan Safronov, a former military correspondent for the newspapers Kommersant and Vedomosti, to 22 years in prison for treason, along with a fine of 500,000 rubles and two years of restricted freedom after release, with eligibility for parole after 14 years. Authorities accused Safronov of spying for a foreign country, but reporting on the case indicated that the classified material he was accused of sharing was already publicly available, and press freedom groups said the prosecution was tied to his 2019 reporting on a planned Russian sale of fighter jets to Egypt, published while he still worked as a journalist. Safronov had been held since his arrest in July 2020 and, as of the sentencing, planned to appeal. The Committee to Protect Journalists' program director, Carlos Martinez de la Serna, said the sentence was unacceptable for a man guilty of no crime other than doing his job as a journalist.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed as a public account of the specific classified material at issue; authorities accused Safronov of spying for a foreign country under Russia's treason law.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A journalist who had reported on Russian military affairs received one of the longest sentences imposed on a Russian journalist in the post-Soviet period, in a case linked by press freedom groups to his earlier reporting rather than any later state role.
incidents.status: Safronov was sentenced to 22 years and planned to appeal; the source reviewed does not report the outcome of any appeal.

incidents.outcome_note: Safronov received a 22-year sentence and planned to appeal; the source reviewed does not report a ruling on any appeal.

incidents.title: Vietnam: journalist Pham Doan Trang is sentenced to nine years for anti-state "propaganda"
incidents.summary: A Vietnamese court sentenced Pham Doan Trang, founding editor of the independent outlet The Vietnamese, to nine years in prison for distributing anti-state "propaganda" under a national-security provision of the country's penal code.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Trang had spent years writing and publishing independent reporting and commentary critical of the ruling Communist Party before her arrest, work for which she had already received international press freedom recognition.

incidents.title: Iran: journalists Niloofar Hamedi and Elahe Mohammadi are sentenced to 13 and 12 years
incidents.summary: Iranian journalists Niloofar Hamedi and Elahe Mohammadi, who broke the story of Mahsa Amini's death in police custody, were sentenced to 13 and 12 years respectively on national-security-linked charges tied to their reporting, and later released on heavy bail.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Hamedi and Mohammadi had reported on the September 2022 death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old woman who died after being held by Iran's morality police for allegedly violating the country's mandatory dress code, reporting that helped ignite months of nationwide protests.
incidents.what_happened: Niloofar Hamedi and Elahe Mohammadi, two Iranian journalists, were sentenced to 13 and 12 years in prison respectively on charges linked to their reporting on the September 2022 hospitalization and death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old woman held by Iran's morality police for allegedly violating the country's mandatory dress code. Hamedi's reporting for the newspaper Shargh and Mohammadi's for the newspaper Ham-Mihan had helped bring the case to national and international attention, contributing to protests that spread across Iran in the months that followed. After spending almost sixteen months in detention, the two journalists were granted bail of about 10 billion tomans, roughly 200,000 dollars, in January 2024, but were also barred from leaving the country. incidents.title: Turkiye: journalist Sedef Kabas is arrested for a proverb about President Erdogan
incidents.summary: Turkish journalist Sedef Kabas was arrested and later convicted under Article 299 of the penal code, which criminalizes insulting the president, after quoting a proverb about a palace becoming a stable during a televised discussion of Erdogan.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Kabas made the comment during a political talk show discussion of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, after also questioning his university diploma and alleging corruption in earlier social media posts.
incidents.what_happened: On January 22, 2022, Turkish police arrested journalist Sedef Kabas from her home after midnight, following comments she made during a televised political talk show in which she said, discussing President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, "When cattle enters a palace, it does not become king but the palace becomes a stable." She was jailed as a flight risk despite her lawyers' objections to the arrest order. Kabas was prosecuted under Article 299 of Turkiye's penal code, which criminalizes insulting the president and carries a sentence of up to four years in prison, with enhanced penalties where the insult is made publicly. She was found guilty and sentenced to two years and four months in prison, and was released pending appeal on March 11, 2022, after 49 days in detention. In June 2023, she faced a further trial on the same Article 299 charge over the same set of remarks, which had also included social media posts questioning Erdogan's university diploma and alleging corruption.
incidents.stated_justification: Turkish prosecutors pursued the case under Article 299 of the penal code, which makes "insulting Turkey's president" a criminal offense.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A journalist was jailed and later convicted over a single televised remark about the president, with a further prosecution on the same charge continuing more than a year later.
incidents.status: Kabas was released pending appeal in March 2022 and faced a new trial on the same charge in June 2023.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not report the final outcome of Kabas's appeal or the 2023 trial.
incidents.outcome_note: Kabas remained free pending appeal as of the sources reviewed, with a further trial on the same Article 299 charge continuing in mid-2023.

incidents.title: Thailand: magazine editor Somyot Prueksakasemsuk is sentenced to 11 years under the lese-majeste law
incidents.summary: A Thai court sentenced magazine editor Somyot Prueksakasemsuk to 11 years in prison under Article 112 of the penal code, the country's lese-majeste law barring insults to the royal family, over two articles he published under a pen name.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The two articles that led to the charge, published in Voice of Taksin magazine in February and March 2010, were written under a pseudonym by a former government spokesman living in exile, whom Somyot identified only after his own prosecution began.
incidents.what_happened: On January 24, 2013, a Thai court sentenced magazine editor Somyot Prueksakasemsuk to 11 years in prison under Article 112 of Thailand's penal code, the country's lese-majeste law, which bars insults to the royal family and under which any Thai person may file a complaint even though royal family members themselves have never personally done so. The charge concerned two articles published in February and March 2010 in Voice of Taksin magazine under the pen name "Jit Polachan." Somyot later identified the true author as Jakrapob Penkair, a former government spokesman then living in exile in Cambodia. During his trial testimony, Somyot argued the articles referred to a broad aristocratic elite rather than the king specifically. CPJ's Asia program coordinator at the time, Bob Dietz, called the sentence the latest abuse of the lese-majeste law to suppress free expression in Thailand. Somyot completed his sentence in full and was released on April 30, 2018, telling reporters the country's military government had led Thailand backward and that he was disappointed democracy had not been restored.
incidents.stated_justification: The prosecution was brought under Article 112 of the penal code, Thailand's lese-majeste law, over the two 2010 magazine articles.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A magazine editor received an 11-year sentence as the person responsible for publication, rather than the pseudonymous author, of two articles a court found insulted the monarchy.
incidents.status: Somyot served his full sentence and was released on April 30, 2018.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not report what happened to Jakrapob Penkair, the article's identified author, who remained in exile.
incidents.outcome_note: Somyot's conviction and sentence were not overturned; he served his full 11-year term and was released on completing it in April 2018.
incidents.ladder_note: An editor received an 11-year sentence under a royal insult law for articles written by someone else, and served the sentence in full before release.

incidents.title: Belarus: journalist Andrzej Poczobut is sentenced to eight years for inciting hatred
incidents.summary: A Belarusian court sentenced dual Belarusian-Polish journalist Andrzej Poczobut to eight years in prison on charges of inciting hatred and calling for sanctions, and he was freed three years later as part of a multi-country prisoner exchange.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Poczobut had been a longtime commentator and producer for programs on the Poland-based independent broadcaster Belsat TV and Polish public broadcaster TVP Polonia, reporting on Belarus for a Polish-speaking audience.
incidents.what_happened: On February 8, 2023, a Belarusian court sentenced journalist Andrzej Poczobut, who holds both Belarusian and Polish citizenship, to eight years in prison on charges of inciting hatred and calling for sanctions said to be aimed at harming Belarus's national security. Poczobut, a political commentator and producer for the program Nad Niemnem on the independent broadcaster Belsat TV and on Polish public broadcaster TVP Polonia, had been imprisoned since March 2021. CPJ's Europe and Central Asia program coordinator, Gulnoza Said, said the sentence illustrated a continuing pattern of Belarusian government action against independent journalists. Poczobut was freed on April 28, 2026, as part of a prisoner exchange involving Poland, Belarus, the United States, Moldova, Romania, Russia, Kazakhstan and Ukraine, in which ten prisoners were swapped at the Polish-Belarusian border. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced the release, calling it the result of a two-year diplomatic effort.

incidents.effect_on_reporting: A journalist covering Belarus for a Polish-speaking audience was imprisoned for about five years before his release depended on a multi-country diplomatic exchange rather than any legal appeal.
incidents.status: Poczobut was freed on April 28, 2026, after about five years in detention, as part of a multi-country prisoner exchange.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not describe the specific statements by Poczobut that Belarusian authorities characterized as inciting hatred.
incidents.outcome_note: Poczobut was freed on April 28, 2026, as part of a prisoner exchange involving eight countries, before completing his eight-year sentence.

incidents.title: Saudi Arabia: spyware on an associate's phone precedes Jamal Khashoggi's killing by one day
incidents.summary: Citizen Lab found Pegasus spyware on the phone of Saudi dissident Omar Abdulaziz, a close associate and collaborator of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, one day before Saudi operatives killed Khashoggi inside the country's Istanbul consulate.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Abdulaziz and Khashoggi had been collaborating on plans for a news and human rights website, and Khashoggi was, according to Abdulaziz, sharply critical of the Saudi crown prince in their private conversations.
incidents.what_happened: On October 1, 2018, the Canadian digital rights research group Citizen Lab published forensic analysis finding, with a high degree of confidence, that Saudi dissident Omar Abdulaziz's phone had been successfully infected with Pegasus spyware made by Israel's NSO Group, in an operation linked to Saudi government operators. Abdulaziz was a close associate of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, and the two had been collaborating on plans for a news and human rights website; Abdulaziz said Khashoggi had been sharply critical of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in their private conversations, including through encrypted messages that the spyware would have exposed. The day after Citizen Lab published its findings, on October 2, 2018, Saudi operatives killed Khashoggi inside the country's consulate in Istanbul. Abdulaziz has said he cannot definitively link the spyware operation against his own phone to Khashoggi's killing, but the timing raised serious questions about how Saudi authorities may have learned of Khashoggi's private communications and views before his death.

incidents.title: Mexico: journalist Carmen Aristegui receives Pegasus spyware through phishing texts
incidents.summary: Citizen Lab, R3D and Article 19 documented Pegasus spyware sent to Mexican investigative journalists Carmen Aristegui and Carlos Loret de Mola through phishing text messages, which the Mexican government denied having sent.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Aristegui and Loret de Mola were among several Mexican investigative journalists, human rights defenders and anti-corruption figures sent the same spyware technique around the same period.

Clicking the links in the messages installed Pegasus spyware, made by the Israeli firm NSO Group, on the recipients' phones. NSO Group has said it sells Pegasus exclusively to governments. President Enrique Pena Nieto's administration categorically denied that any of its members engaged in surveillance or communications operations against human rights defenders, journalists or anti-corruption activists without prior judicial authorization. Citizen Lab's report said the spyware itself could not be traced back to whoever had sent it, and that there was no conclusive evidence establishing who was responsible.
